title: Identifying ions
aim: To use chemical tests (flame tests, sodium hydroxide solution, and tests for carbonate, halide and sulfate ions) to identify the positive and negative ions in unknown ionic compounds.
background: Flame tests identify some metal ions from the colour they give to a flame: lithium is crimson, sodium is yellow, potassium is lilac, calcium is orange-red and copper is green. If a sample contains a mixture of ions, some flame colours may be hidden by others (for example, yellow sodium masks other colours).

Sodium hydroxide solution forms insoluble metal hydroxide precipitates with some metal ions. Aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions form white precipitates; only aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide. Copper(II) forms a blue precipitate, iron(II) a green precipitate and iron(III) a brown precipitate. For example: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s).

Carbonate ions react with dilute acid to produce carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky (cloudy). Halide ions form precipitates with silver nitrate solution in the presence of dilute nitric acid: silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow. Sulfate ions form a white precipitate of barium sulfate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.

The acids are added first to remove carbonate ions, which would otherwise also form precipitates and give a false positive. Nitric acid is used for the halide test and hydrochloric acid for the sulfate test so that no extra halide or sulfate ions are added.
hypothesis: Each unknown compound will give a characteristic result for its metal ion (flame colour or hydroxide precipitate colour) and for its negative ion (gas or precipitate), allowing both ions to be identified.

variables.independent: The unknown compound being tested (samples A to H).
variables.dependent: The observations: flame colour, colour of hydroxide precipitate and whether it dissolves in excess, and the result of each negative ion test.
control: Volume of sample solution used in each test (about 2 cm³ in a test tube)
Concentration of test reagents (dilute sodium hydroxide, silver nitrate, barium chloride, acids)
Number of drops of reagent added before observing
Cleaning the flame test loop between samples
Same part of the Bunsen flame (edge of a blue, roaring flame)

equipment: Nichrome (or platinum) wire loop in a holder
Watch glass of dilute hydrochloric acid (for cleaning the loop)
Test tubes and test tube rack
Dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute nitric acid
Silver nitrate solution (0.05 mol/dm³) and barium chloride solution (0.1 mol/dm³)
Limewater and a delivery tube with bung (or a pipette to transfer gas)
Unknown solids and solutions A to H
method: Flame test: clean a nichrome wire loop by dipping it in dilute hydrochloric acid and holding it in a hot Bunsen flame until it gives no colour.

Dip the clean loop into the hydrochloric acid and then into a small sample of the solid. Hold it at the edge of a blue (roaring) Bunsen flame and record the flame colour. Clean the loop again before testing the next sample.
Hydroxide test: put about 2 cm³ of a solution of the sample into a test tube. Add a few drops of dilute sodium hydroxide solution and record the colour of any precipitate.

If a white precipitate forms, keep adding sodium hydroxide solution until it is in excess. Record whether the precipitate dissolves (aluminium) or stays (calcium or magnesium; use the flame test to tell these apart).

Carbonate test: put a small amount of the sample in a test tube and add about 2 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid. If it fizzes, pass the gas through limewater using a delivery tube. Record whether the limewater turns milky.
Halide test: put about 2 cm³ of a solution of the sample into a test tube. Add a few drops of dilute nitric acid, then a few drops of silver nitrate solution. Record the colour of any precipitate.

Sulfate test: put about 2 cm³ of a solution of the sample into a test tube. Add a few drops of dilute hydrochloric acid, then a few drops of barium chloride solution. Record whether a white precipitate forms.
Repeat all the tests for each unknown sample, using clean test tubes and pipettes each time.
Use your results table to identify the positive ion and the negative ion in each sample, and name each compound.
Dispose of solutions containing silver and barium compounds in the waste containers provided.

safety.risk: Irritant or corrosive to eyes and skin.
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection, use dilute solution and wash splashes off skin immediately.
Use dilute solution, never pipette by mouth, wash hands after use and dispose of in the labelled waste container.

safety.risk: Irritant to eyes and stains skin black; harmful to the environment.
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection, avoid skin contact and dispose of in the labelled waste container.

safety.hazard: Bunsen burner and hot wire loop
safety.risk: Burns from the flame or hot wire; acid on the loop may spit.
safety.precaution: Hold the loop by its insulated handle, tie back hair, and let the wire cool on a heatproof mat.
Wear eye protection and wash splashes off with water.

rows: Dilute HCl: fizzes, gas turns limewater milky
White precipitate, does not dissolve in excess
results.notes: Identify the positive ion from the flame test and/or the hydroxide precipitate, and the negative ion from the carbonate, halide or sulfate test. A white hydroxide precipitate that does not dissolve in excess could be calcium or magnesium: a flame test distinguishes them (calcium is orange-red, magnesium gives no colour).

analysis: Sample A gave a crimson flame, so it contains lithium ions (Li⁺). The cream precipitate with silver nitrate shows bromide ions (Br⁻). A is lithium bromide.

Sample B gave a blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide (Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s)) and a green flame, so it contains copper(II) ions. The white precipitate with barium chloride shows sulfate ions: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s). B is copper(II) sulfate.

Samples C and G both gave white hydroxide precipitates. Only C's dissolved in excess sodium hydroxide, so C contains aluminium ions. G's did not, and G gave an orange-red flame, so G contains calcium ions. Both gave white precipitates with silver nitrate, showing chloride ions: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).
Sample E gave a green precipitate (iron(II) hydroxide) and sample H a brown precipitate (iron(III) hydroxide), so the two iron compounds can be told apart by the colour of their hydroxides.

Sample D fizzed with acid and the gas turned limewater milky, so it contains carbonate ions (CO₃²⁻); the lilac flame shows potassium ions. Sample F gave a yellow flame (sodium ions) and a yellow precipitate with silver nitrate (iodide ions).

errors.error: A dirty flame test loop carries over ions from the previous sample, giving the wrong flame colour.
errors.improvement: Clean the loop in hydrochloric acid and heat it until it gives no colour before every test.

errors.error: Flame colours are subjective, and in a mixture one colour can hide another (for example sodium's yellow masks lilac potassium).
errors.improvement: Use flame emission spectroscopy, an instrumental method that identifies each metal ion from its line spectrum and works with mixtures.

errors.error: Adding too little sodium hydroxide means an aluminium hydroxide precipitate is not seen to dissolve, so aluminium is mistaken for calcium or magnesium.
errors.improvement: Add sodium hydroxide drop by drop and then keep adding until clearly in excess, shaking after each addition.

errors.error: The colours of silver halide precipitates (white, cream, yellow) can be hard to tell apart.
errors.improvement: Compare the precipitate side by side with results from known chloride, bromide and iodide solutions against a white background.

errors.error: Carbonate ions in the sample can form precipitates with silver nitrate or barium chloride, giving a false positive.
errors.improvement: Always add the dilute acid (nitric for halides, hydrochloric for sulfates) before the test reagent, to remove carbonate ions.

examTips: Learn the flame colours as a list: lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper green.
Learn the hydroxide colours: Cu²⁺ blue, Fe²⁺ green, Fe³⁺ brown; Al³⁺, Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ white, and only Al³⁺ dissolves in excess.
Give both the reagent and the result for each test: for example 'add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution: a white precipitate shows chloride ions'.

Explain the acids: they remove carbonate ions that would give a false positive. Use nitric acid (not hydrochloric) for halides and hydrochloric acid (not sulfuric) for sulfates, so you do not add the ion you are testing for.
Write balanced ionic equations with state symbols for precipitate reactions, for example Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s).

questions.question:
A student does flame tests on solutions of four metal ions.
Which metal ion gives a lilac flame?
markScheme: 1 mark: potassium (K⁺)
questions.explanation: Potassium gives lilac. Lithium is crimson, sodium is yellow and calcium is orange-red.

questions.question:
A student adds sodium hydroxide solution to a solution of an unknown compound. A green precipitate forms.
Which metal ion is present in the compound?
markScheme: 1 mark: iron(II), Fe²⁺
questions.explanation: Iron(II) hydroxide is green. Copper(II) hydroxide is blue, iron(III) hydroxide is brown and aluminium hydroxide is white.

questions.explanation: Carbonates react with acids to make carbon dioxide. Carbon dioxide is identified because it turns limewater milky.

questions.question:
A student adds dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution to a solution. A yellow precipitate forms.
Which ion is present in the solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: iodide, I⁻
questions.explanation: Silver iodide is yellow, silver bromide is cream and silver chloride is white. Sulfate is tested with barium chloride, not silver nitrate.

questions.question: Describe how to test a solution for sulfate ions. Give the reagents and the positive result.
markScheme: 1 mark: add dilute hydrochloric acid followed by barium chloride solution
1 mark: a white precipitate (of barium sulfate) forms
questions.explanation: The acid is added first to remove carbonate ions, which would also form a white precipitate with barium ions.

questions.question:
A student adds sodium hydroxide solution to two solutions, X and Y.
Table 1 shows the results.
Identify the metal ion in X.
Give two possible metal ions in Y.

headers: Observation with a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution
Observation with excess sodium hydroxide solution

markScheme: 1 mark: X contains aluminium ions (Al³⁺)
1 mark: Y contains calcium ions (Ca²⁺) or magnesium ions (Mg²⁺)
questions.explanation: Aluminium hydroxide is the only white hydroxide that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide. A flame test would distinguish calcium (orange-red) from magnesium (no colour).

questions.question:
A student tests a solution for halide ions.
Explain why the student must not use hydrochloric acid to acidify the solution.
markScheme: 1 mark: hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions
1 mark: which would form a white precipitate with silver nitrate (false positive for chloride)
questions.explanation: Nitric acid is used because nitrate ions do not form a precipitate with silver ions. Adding chloride ions would always give a white precipitate.

acceptedAnswers: heat in flame until no colour
markScheme: 1 mark: dip the loop in (dilute hydrochloric) acid and hold in a hot Bunsen flame until it gives no colour
1 mark: to remove ions from previous samples, which would give the wrong flame colour (contamination)
questions.explanation: Even a trace of another metal ion, especially sodium, can change or mask the flame colour.

questions.question:
A student does two tests on a solid compound.
Table 1 shows the results.
What is the compound?

rows: Dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution added to a solution of the solid

markScheme: 1 mark: calcium chloride
questions.explanation: Orange-red shows calcium ions, and a white silver halide precipitate shows chloride ions. Bromide would give a cream precipitate; lithium gives a crimson flame.

questions.question: Which is the correct ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of iron(III) ions with sodium hydroxide solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s)
questions.explanation: Iron(III) has a 3+ charge, so three hydroxide ions are needed. The precipitate is a solid (s). The Fe²⁺ equation describes iron(II), which gives a green precipitate.

questions.question:
A student does a flame test on a mixture of sodium chloride and potassium chloride and sees only a yellow flame.
Explain this result and suggest a better method for identifying the metal ions in the mixture.
markScheme: 1 mark: the bright yellow colour of sodium masks / hides the lilac colour of potassium
1 mark: use flame emission spectroscopy (an instrumental method that identifies each ion from its spectrum)
questions.explanation: Flame tests work poorly with mixtures. Flame emission spectroscopy gives a line spectrum for each metal ion, so it can identify ions in a mixture and also measure their concentrations.

questions.question:
The white precipitate formed in the test for sulfate ions is barium sulfate, BaSO₄.
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of barium sulfate.
Table 1 shows the relative atomic masses (Ar) of the elements.
questions.explanation: Mr = 137 + 32 + 64 = 233. Remember there are four oxygen atoms in the sulfate ion.

questions.question: What colour precipitate forms when sodium hydroxide solution is added to copper(II) sulfate solution?
markScheme: 1 mark: blue
questions.explanation: Copper(II) hydroxide is a blue precipitate. The solution itself is also blue, so look for the solid forming, not just the colour.

questions.question:
A student does tests on a white solid.
Table 1 shows the results.
Identify the compound.
Write a balanced equation for the reaction of the compound with hydrochloric acid.

rows: Dilute hydrochloric acid added to the solid

markScheme: 1 mark: lithium carbonate (Li₂CO₃)
1 mark: correct formulae: Li₂CO₃ + HCl → LiCl + H₂O + CO₂
1 mark: balanced: Li₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2LiCl + H₂O + CO₂
questions.explanation: Crimson identifies lithium, and carbon dioxide gas from acid identifies carbonate. Lithium forms Li⁺ ions and carbonate is CO₃²⁻, so the formula is Li₂CO₃.

questions.question:
A student has three unlabelled solutions: iron(II) sulfate, iron(III) chloride and copper(II) chloride.
Describe how the student could use chemical tests to identify each solution. Give the expected results.
markScheme: Indicative content: put a small sample of each solution in separate test tubes; add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution; iron(II) gives a green precipitate, iron(III) gives a brown precipitate, copper(II) gives a blue precipitate; to confirm negative ions, take fresh samples; add dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride solution: white precipitate shows sulfate (iron(II) sulfate); add dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution: white precipitate shows chloride (iron(III) chloride and copper(II) chloride); copper could also be confirmed by a green flame test; use clean apparatus for each test
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent plan that uses sodium hydroxide to distinguish all three metal ions with correct colours, and also confirms the negative ions with the correct reagents and results.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): uses sodium hydroxide with mostly correct colours, or correct negative ion tests with some metal ion results; some detail missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names a relevant test or gives one correct result, with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Sodium hydroxide alone can tell all three apart because the metal ions give different coloured precipitates. Confirming the anions with fresh samples shows full understanding of the tests.
